etymology: From the Latin doctrina, “teaching,” here the church’s confession of who God is in Himself: one in essence, three in Person, perfect and unchanging.
biblical_def: The doctrine of God is the church’s confession of the LORD as He has revealed Himself: the one living and true God, infinite in being and perfection, a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions. He is from Himself and of Himself, deriving His being from none; when Moses asked His name, He answered, “I AM THAT I AM” (Exo 3:14), the self-existent and self-sufficient One. He is one in essence: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4); yet that one God subsists eternally in three Persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, of one substance, power, and eternity. Because His being is perfect, He is simple, not compounded of parts, but wholly what He is; His attributes are not pieces added to Him but His very essence. He is immutable, the same yesterday, today, and for ever: “I am the LORD, I change not” (Mal 3:6). He neither grows nor learns nor repents as men do, neither is moved against His will by the creature. Being spirit, He must be worshipped in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:24). This God of aseity, simplicity, immutability, and triunity is the God of Scripture and of the whole catholic faith, the rock that does not shift beneath His people.
webster_summary: The church’s confession of the one living God, self-existent, simple, immutable, and one in three Persons.
webster_full: DOCTRINE OF GOD, the church’s teaching concerning the being and attributes of the LORD.
He is self-existent, deriving His being from none: “I AM THAT I AM” (Exo 3:14).
He is one in essence and three in Person, of one substance and eternity.
He is simple and immutable, without parts or passions: “I change not” (Mal 3:6).
Being spirit, He must be worshipped in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:24).
scriptures: Exo 3:14
And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
Deu 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:
Mal 3:6
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: Open theism and process theology corrupt the doctrine of God, fashioning a mutable, learning, therapeutic deity in place of the immutable LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the remaking of God after the image of man. Open theism (Pinnock, Boyd, Sanders) denies that God exhaustively foreknows the free future, making Him a deity who waits, hopes, and is genuinely surprised. Process theism goes further, denying immutability and omnipotence outright, so that God grows and develops along with the world. Both are answered flatly by Malachi 3:6, “I am the LORD, I change not,” and by Exodus 3:14, the name of the self-existent One who depends on nothing. A God who changes, learns, or is overpowered by the creature is not the God of Scripture but an idol of the modern imagination.

Alongside these stands the therapeutic, progressive remaking of God into a being whose chief attribute is unconditional affirmation, a deity emptied of holiness, wrath, and unchanging justice, refashioned to flatter the worshipper rather than to be worshipped. This too is rejected. The God of the Bible is impassible, not moved about by His creatures’ moods, and immutable in His holiness as in His mercy. To trade the great I AM for a mutable, comforting projection is to break the first commandment in the very act of theology. The dictionary holds the classical attributes — aseity, simplicity, immutability, impassibility, triunity — against every modern softening.
roots_summary: The doctrine confesses God as self-existent, one in essence, three in Person, simple and immutable.
roots_lines: Aseity — God is from Himself, deriving His being from none (Exo 3:14).
Unity — the LORD our God is one LORD (Deu 6:4).
Triunity — one essence subsisting in Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.
Simplicity — God is not compounded of parts; His attributes are His essence.
Immutability — He changes not, the same for ever (Mal 3:6).
usage: Because the LORD changes not, His people rest on a rock that does not shift beneath them.
The God who is from Himself needs nothing from us; we worship Him for who He is, not for what He gives.
To worship the great I AM is to refuse every mutable, therapeutic idol the age would put in His place.

etymology: From the Greek anthropos, “man,” and logos, “word” or “study”; the doctrine of man as God made him, fell, and redeems him.
biblical_def: Biblical anthropology is the doctrine of man as the Scriptures teach it. Man is not a product of chance but a creature fashioned by God in His own image: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them” (Gen 1:27). He is a unity of body and soul, formed of the dust of the ground and made a living soul by the breath of God: “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7). Thus man is neither a bare animal nor a disembodied spirit, but body and soul together, made for fellowship with his Maker. He was crowned with dignity above the beasts, set a little lower than the angels and given dominion over the works of God’s hands (Psa 8:4–5). Yet this image-bearer fell in Adam, his federal head, so that sin and death passed upon all: “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Rom 5:12). Man is therefore at once gloriously made and deeply fallen, the image of God defaced but not destroyed, male and female in their created order, body and soul awaiting either resurrection to life or to judgment. The whole hope of fallen man is the second Adam, Christ, in whom the image is restored.
webster_summary: The doctrine of man as God’s image-bearer, body and soul, male and female, created good and fallen in Adam.
webster_full: BIBLICAL ANTHROPOLOGY, the Scripture’s doctrine of the nature and estate of man.
Man is made in the image of God, male and female (Gen 1:27).
He is a unity of body and soul, dust quickened by God’s breath (Gen 2:7).
He is crowned with dignity above the beasts, a little lower than the angels (Psa 8:4–5).
He fell in Adam, so that sin and death passed upon all men (Rom 5:12).
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Gen 2:7
And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Psa 8:4
What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
corruption_summary: Evolutionary materialism and gender ideology corrupt biblical anthropology, denying both the Creator who made man and the embodied sex in which He made him.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption comes from two quarters. The first is evolutionary materialism, which denies that man is a creature made in God’s image and reduces him to an advanced animal, a momentary arrangement of matter without soul, dignity, or moral accountability. Against this stands Genesis 2:7, where man is dust quickened by the breath of God into a living soul, and Psalm 8, where he is crowned with glory and honour above the beasts. Man did not climb up from the brute; he was made upright by God and fell from that height in Adam. To deny the Creator is to lose the very ground of human worth.

The second corruption is gender ideology, which detaches a person’s claimed identity from his or her embodied sex, treating maleness and femaleness as feelings to be chosen rather than a creational order to be received. This is a direct corruption of Genesis 1:27: “male and female created he them.” Sex is the embodied, immutable category in which God made every image-bearer; it is given, not assigned, and not subject to revision. The dictionary affirms the dignity of every person as God’s image-bearer while naming the gender-identity claim as a denial of how that image was made. Pastoral compassion for those in distress never requires assenting to a falsehood about the body God gave.
roots_summary: Man is God’s image-bearer, body and soul, male and female, made good and fallen in Adam.
roots_lines: Image — man made in the image of God (Gen 1:27).
Body and soul — dust quickened into a living soul (Gen 2:7).
Male and female — the created, embodied order of the sexes.
Dignity — crowned above the beasts, a little lower than the angels (Psa 8:5).
Fallen — sin and death entered by one man, Adam (Rom 5:12).
usage: Because man is God’s image-bearer, every human life is sacred from the womb to the grave.
The unity of body and soul forbids us to despise the body or to worship it; both are made for God.
Man fallen in Adam can be restored only in the second Adam, Christ, in whom the image is made new.

etymology: From the Latin sacramentum, a sacred oath or pledge; the church’s name for the two ordinances Christ appointed as visible signs and seals of His covenant.
biblical_def: The sacraments, more exactly called ordinances, are the two holy signs Christ Himself appointed for His church: baptism and the Lord’s Supper. They are not bare ceremonies but signs and seals of the covenant of grace, by which the benefits of Christ are visibly set forth, and the faith of believers strengthened. Baptism was commanded by the risen Lord: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19). It signifies the believer’s union with Christ in His death and resurrection, the washing away of sin, and engrafting into His body. The Supper was instituted by Christ on the night He was betrayed, when He took bread and the cup and said, “Take, eat; this is my body… this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins” (Mat 26:26–28). In it the church shows the Lord’s death till He come (1Co 11:23–26), and believers feed upon Christ by faith, receiving His spiritual presence and the renewal of covenant communion. Peter joined repentance and baptism in the first gospel call (Act 2:38). Both ordinances are signs that point beyond themselves to Christ crucified and risen, seals that pledge to faith the grace they signify, and means by which the Lord nourishes His people.
webster_summary: The two ordinances of Christ, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, signs and seals of the covenant of grace.
webster_full: SACRAMENTS (ORDINANCES), the two holy signs Christ appointed for His church.
Baptism, commanded by the risen Lord, signifies union with Christ (Mat 28:19).
The Lord’s Supper, instituted the night He was betrayed, shows His death (Mat 26:26–28).
They are signs and seals of the covenant, not bare ceremonies.
In them believers feed on Christ by faith and are strengthened (1Co 11:23–26).
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body.
Act 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
corruption_summary: Rome’s transubstantiation and seven-sacrament system and the doctrine of baptismal regeneration corrupt the ordinances, as does bare memorialism that empties them of Christ’s spiritual presence.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman church corrupted the ordinances in several ways. It multiplied the two Christ appointed into seven, adding confirmation, penance, extreme unction, orders, and marriage to baptism and the Supper without warrant of His institution. It taught transubstantiation, that the bread and wine cease to be bread and wine and become the very body and blood of Christ in substance, so that the Mass is offered anew as a propitiatory sacrifice — a doctrine that contradicts Hebrews’ one offering once for all and turns the Supper into an idolatrous re-sacrificing of Christ. It taught baptismal regeneration, that the water itself confers the new birth apart from faith, making the sign the thing signified. The Reformation recovered the two ordinances of Christ as signs and seals received by faith, not works that save by their bare performance.

The opposite error must also be rejected. Bare Zwinglian memorialism reduces the Supper to a mere remembrance, a token of bread and wine signifying nothing but a past event, denying that Christ is truly present to faith and truly feeds His people in the ordinance. Against both Rome and the bare-memorial view, the dictionary holds the Reformed position: the Supper is a sign and seal in which the believer, by faith, spiritually feeds upon the crucified and risen Christ and is knit afresh into covenant communion with Him. The ordinances do not save by their working; neither are they empty. They are Christ’s appointed means of grace, where He meets His people.
roots_summary: Two ordinances of Christ, baptism and the Supper, signs and seals of the covenant of grace.
roots_lines: Sacramentum — Latin, a sacred oath or pledge.
Baptism — commanded by the risen Lord (Mat 28:19).
Lord’s Supper — instituted the night Christ was betrayed (Mat 26:26).
Sign — visibly setting forth the benefits of Christ.
Seal — pledging to faith the grace it signifies.
usage: The ordinances preach Christ to the eye as the word preaches Him to the ear.
Receive the Supper by faith, feeding on Christ, not by a bare remembrance nor a Romish re-sacrifice.
Baptism marks the believer’s union with Christ; it does not regenerate by the water itself.

etymology: The study of God’s self-revelation as it unfolds through Scripture in redemptive history, with Christ as its centre and end.
biblical_def: Biblical theology is the discipline that traces the unfolding of God’s redemptive purpose through the whole of Scripture, from promise to fulfilment, finding in Christ the centre and end of all. It is not a patchwork of unrelated books but one story of redemption, told in many ages, with one Author and one great theme. The risen Lord Himself taught this on the road to Emmaus: “beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27). He charged the Jews that the very Scriptures they searched testified of Him: “they are they which testify of me” (Joh 5:39). The prophets who foretold the grace to come searched diligently, “searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow” (1Pe 1:10–11). And all of it, every age and every book, is breathed out by God: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). Biblical theology therefore reads the Old Testament as the seed and shadow of the New, and the New as the flower and substance of the Old, with Christ crucified and risen as the key that opens the whole. It guards the unity of the canon and the centrality of Christ against every reading that would fragment the word of God.
webster_summary: The study of God’s redemptive revelation as it unfolds through Scripture, with Christ as the centre of all.
webster_full: BIBLICAL THEOLOGY, the tracing of God’s redemptive purpose through the whole of Scripture.
The risen Christ expounded all the Scriptures concerning Himself (Luk 24:27).
The Scriptures testify of Christ from first to last (Joh 5:39).
The prophets foretold the sufferings of Christ and the glory to follow (1Pe 1:10–11).
All Scripture is breathed out by God, one word with one Author (2Ti 3:16).
scriptures: And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Liberal higher criticism corrupts biblical theology, fragmenting the canon by the documentary hypothesis and denying the one Author who centred all Scripture on Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is liberal higher criticism, which fractures the unity of Scripture into a heap of competing human sources. The documentary hypothesis carves the books of Moses into supposed strands woven together by later editors, denying that Moses wrote the Torah; parallel schemes invent a second and third Isaiah, a Daniel written centuries after the prophet, and Gospels recast as late legends. By this method the Scripture ceases to be one word from one Author and becomes a museum of religious fragments. Against it stands 2 Timothy 3:16: all Scripture is given by inspiration of God. The Spirit of Christ spoke through every writer (1Pe 1:11); the word is not a stitching of human guesses but the breath of God.

The deeper error of this scholarship is that, having fragmented the canon, it loses its centre. Where Christ said the Scriptures testify of Him (Joh 5:39) and expounded Himself out of all of them (Luk 24:27), higher criticism reads each fragment as the religion of its age, with no unfolding plan and no Redeemer at the centre. The dictionary rejects this fragmenting method root and branch. Scripture is one book, with Christ crucified and risen as its theme from Genesis to Revelation; biblical theology is the reverent tracing of that one redemptive story, not the dismantling of it into sources that never confess the Lord.
roots_summary: One unfolding story of redemption, breathed out by God, centred on Christ from first to last.
roots_lines: Unfolding — redemption revealed by stages from promise to fulfilment.
Centre — Christ, of whom all the Scriptures testify (Joh 5:39).
Continuity — the Old Testament the seed, the New the flower.
Inspiration — all Scripture breathed out by God (2Ti 3:16).
Unity — one Author, one word, against every fragmenting method.
usage: Read every part of Scripture toward Christ, for all of it testifies of Him.
The Old Testament is not a discarded religion but the shadow of the substance now come in Christ.
Hold the unity of the canon against every scheme that would saw it into rival human sources.

etymology: From the Old English godspell, “good news,” rendering the Greek euangelion; the good news of Christ crucified, buried, and risen for sinners.
biblical_def: The gospel is the good news of salvation accomplished by Jesus Christ for sinners, received by faith alone. Paul gives its very content: “Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures” (1Co 15:3–4). This is the heart of the message: a crucified, buried, and risen Saviour, who bore the wrath of God in the room of His people and was raised for their justification. The gospel is the power of God unto salvation, “for therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith” (Rom 1:16–17), for in it God justifies the ungodly, not by works but by faith. Salvation is by grace through faith, and that not of ourselves: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:8–9). God is shown to be both just and the justifier of him that believeth in Jesus, being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Rom 3:24–26). The gospel is therefore not advice but news, not a programme of self-improvement but the announcement of a finished work: that God has reconciled sinners to Himself through the cross and empty tomb of His Son, and freely accounts righteous all who trust in Him.
webster_summary: The good news of Christ crucified, buried, and risen, by whom sinners are justified through faith alone.
webster_full: THE GOSPEL, the good news of salvation accomplished by Jesus Christ.
Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose the third day (1Co 15:3–4).
It is the power of God unto salvation, righteousness revealed to faith (Rom 1:16–17).
Salvation is by grace through faith, not of works (Eph 2:8–9).
God is just and the justifier of him that believeth in Jesus (Rom 3:24–26).
scriptures: For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Rom 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
corruption_summary: The social gospel, the prosperity gospel, and every works-righteousness corrupt the gospel, exchanging Christ crucified and faith alone for human striving or earthly gain.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption takes several modern shapes. The social gospel hollows out the cross, recasting salvation as the reform of society and the bettering of earthly conditions, until sin, atonement, and the new birth drop away and the gospel becomes a programme of moral and political improvement. The prosperity gospel debases it the other way, promising health and wealth to those with faith enough to claim them, making Christ a means to earthly gain rather than the Saviour from sin and wrath. Both forget that the gospel is “Christ died for our sins” (1Co 15:3), a finished work for guilty sinners, not a lever for worldly betterment.

Beneath all these lies the ancient corruption of works-righteousness, the belief that a man is justified, in whole or in part, by his own obedience, merit, sacraments, or striving. This is the very error the Reformation answered with sola fide. Ephesians 2:8–9 forecloses it: salvation is by grace through faith, the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast. Romans shows God to be both just and the justifier of him that believeth in Jesus, justified freely by grace through the redemption in Christ (Rom 3:24–26). The dictionary holds the true gospel: a crucified, buried, and risen Christ received by faith alone, His righteousness imputed, all of grace, to the glory of God alone.
roots_summary: Christ crucified, buried, and risen, received by faith alone, justifying sinners freely by grace.
roots_lines: Godspell — Old English, “good news.”
Crucified — Christ died for our sins (1Co 15:3).
Risen — raised the third day according to the Scriptures.
Faith alone — by grace are ye saved through faith (Eph 2:8).
Imputed — God just and the justifier of the believer (Rom 3:26).
usage: The gospel is news of a finished work, not advice toward self-improvement.
Preach Christ crucified and risen; neither social reform nor prosperity is the good news.
Rest wholly on Christ’s righteousness received by faith, that no man may boast in his works.

etymology: From the Old English hælan, “to make whole”; the doctrine of God as the healer of His people, body and soul, in His providence and in Christ.
biblical_def: The doctrine of healing confesses that the LORD is the healer of His people, who appoints both sickness and health in His wise providence, and who has purchased in Christ a healing that is ultimate and sure. God revealed Himself to Israel as healer: “I am the LORD that healeth thee” (Exo 15:26). The psalmist blesses Him who “forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases” (Psa 103:2–3), joining the healing of the body to the deeper healing of the soul from sin. The suffering Servant bore the chastisement of His people’s peace: “with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5), a word that reaches first to the healing of the soul from sin and finally to the redemption of the body. The church is taught to pray for the sick: “Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him… and the prayer of faith shall save the sick” (Jas 5:14–15). Thus the dictionary holds that God truly heals, in answer to prayer and by ordinary means, as it pleases Him; that sickness comes under His providence, sometimes for chastening, sometimes for His glory, sometimes simply as part of the groaning creation; and that the full and certain healing the atonement secures is the resurrection of the body, when the redeemed shall be raised incorruptible and death itself swallowed up in victory.
webster_summary: The doctrine that God heals His people in His providence, and that the atonement’s final healing is the resurrection.
webster_full: DOCTRINE OF HEALING, the teaching that God is the healer of His people.
He revealed Himself as “the LORD that healeth thee” (Exo 15:26).
He heals diseases of the body and forgives the iniquities of the soul (Psa 103:2–3).
By Christ’s stripes His people are healed (Isa 53:5).
The church prays for the sick, leaving the issue to God’s will (Jas 5:14–15).
scriptures: And said, If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, and wilt do that which is right in his sight, and wilt give ear to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of these diseases upon thee, which I have brought upon the Egyptians: for I am the LORD that healeth thee.
Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases;
Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Jas 5:14
Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord:
corruption_summary: Word-faith “always-heal” teaching and the prosperity-health gospel corrupt the doctrine of healing, denying God’s providence over sickness and blaming the sufferer’s faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the word-faith and prosperity-health movement, which teaches that healing is guaranteed in this life to all who have faith enough to claim it, and that any believer who remains sick has failed to believe. This is a cruel error. It denies that sickness comes under God’s providence, ignores that the apostle Paul was left with a thorn in the flesh and Timothy with his often infirmities, and turns the prayer of faith into a manipulative formula that commands God rather than submits to Him. James teaches the church to pray for the sick and leave the issue to the Lord’s will (Jas 5:14–15); he does not promise that every prayer of faith ends in bodily cure, but that it commits the sick into God’s merciful hand.

The deeper corruption is the misreading of Isaiah 53:5, “with his stripes we are healed,” as a blank cheque for present bodily health. Peter himself applies that verse to the healing of the soul from sin: “by whose stripes ye were healed,” having just said Christ bore our sins in His own body. The atonement does secure the healing of the body, but ultimately, in the resurrection, when the redeemed are raised incorruptible. The faith-healer who blames the sick for their sickness has exchanged the God who appoints affliction for His people’s good for an idol who must perform on demand. The dictionary holds that God heals as He wills, that suffering is under His providence, and that the sure healing of the body is the resurrection.
roots_summary: God heals His people in providence; the atonement’s final healing is the raising of the body.
roots_lines: Hælan — Old English, “to make whole.”
The LORD that healeth — God revealed as healer (Exo 15:26).
Soul and body — He forgives iniquity and heals disease (Psa 103:3).
Providence — sickness appointed for chastening, glory, or the groaning creation.
Resurrection — the atonement’s ultimate healing of the body.
usage: Pray for the sick in faith, yet leave the issue to the Lord’s wise and merciful will.
Sickness is no proof of weak faith; God appoints affliction to His people for their good.
The sure healing the cross secures is the resurrection of the body, not a guaranteed present cure.

etymology: Hebrew Immanu’el, “God with us,” the prophetic name of the virgin-born Son, the incarnate God.
biblical_def: Immanuel, “God with us,” is the prophetic name given to the promised Son, and confessed by the church as the doctrine of the incarnation: that the eternal Son of God took to Himself a true human nature, born of a virgin, so that God Himself came to dwell among His people. Isaiah foretold it as a sign: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (Isa 7:14). Matthew records the fulfilment in the conception of Christ by the Holy Ghost in the womb of the virgin Mary, “and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us” (Mat 1:23). John declares the mystery plainly: “the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory” (Joh 1:14) — the eternal Word, who was God, took flesh without ceasing to be God. Paul shows the depth of His humbling: being in the form of God, He “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men” (Php 2:6–7). In Immanuel two whole natures, the divine and the human, are united in one Person, without confusion, change, division, or separation. He is very God of very God, and very man of the substance of His mother, that He might be the Mediator between God and men. The name Immanuel is the gospel in two words: God Himself, with us, to save us.
webster_summary: “God with us”: the virgin-born incarnate Son, very God and very man in one Person.
webster_full: IMMANUEL, Hebrew for “God with us,” the name of the incarnate Son.
Isaiah foretold the virgin-born sign called Immanuel (Isa 7:14).
Matthew records its fulfilment in Christ, “God with us” (Mat 1:23).
The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (Joh 1:14).
He took the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men (Php 2:6–7).
scriptures: Isa 7:14
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Mat 1:23
Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.
Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Php 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
corruption_summary: Denial of the virgin birth and of Christ’s true deity corrupts Immanuel, leaving a merely human Jesus who is not God with us at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the denial of the virgin birth, whether by liberal scholarship that dismisses Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23 as legend, or by any teaching that makes Jesus the natural son of Joseph. To deny the virgin conception is to deny the manner God appointed for the Son to take flesh and to undercut the sign Isaiah gave. Matthew is plain that Mary was found with child of the Holy Ghost before she and Joseph came together; the conception was the work of the Spirit, not of man. The dictionary affirms the virgin birth as the Scripture teaches it, the fitting entrance of the sinless Son into our nature.

The deeper corruption is the denial of Christ’s true deity, the ancient error renewed in every age that reduces Him to a great teacher, a prophet, or a created being — an Arianism that empties Immanuel of its meaning. If Christ is not God, then He is not God with us, and the Word was not made flesh. John says the Word was God and was made flesh (Joh 1:1, 14); Paul says He was in the form of God and took the form of a servant (Php 2:6–7). The Chalcedonian confession guards the truth: one Person in two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation. To strip away His Godhead is to lose the gospel, for only God with us can save us.
roots_summary: “God with us”: the virgin-born Son, very God and very man, one Person in two natures.
roots_lines: Immanu’el — Hebrew, “God with us.”
Sign — a virgin shall conceive and bear a son (Isa 7:14).
Fulfilment — Christ conceived of the Holy Ghost (Mat 1:23).
Incarnation — the Word made flesh, dwelling among us (Joh 1:14).
Humbling — He took the form of a servant (Php 2:7).
usage: In Immanuel the eternal God draws near to dwell with His people and to save them.
Hold both natures of Christ: very God and very man, one Person, our only Mediator.
To deny His virgin birth or His Godhead is to lose the God-with-us who alone can save.

etymology: From the Latin protegere, “to cover, to shield”; the doctrine of God’s providential keeping of His people as shield, refuge, and fortress.
biblical_def: Divine protection is the doctrine that God in His providence guards and keeps His people, being their shield, refuge, and fortress against every evil. The psalmist confesses, “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust” (Psa 91:1–2). The LORD keeps the going out and the coming in of His own: “The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul. The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore” (Psa 121:7–8). His name itself is a stronghold: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). And the apostle assures the saints that “the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil” (2Th 3:3). This protection is real and sure, but it is the protection of providence, not a charm against all earthly harm. God keeps His people unto His kingdom; He preserves their souls without fail and their bodies according to His wise purpose. The same God who shielded David let the prophets be sawn asunder and the martyrs be slain, working all for their eternal good. The doctrine teaches the saint to trust in the LORD as his refuge while bowing to whatever providence He appoints.
webster_summary: The doctrine that God providentially keeps His people as shield, refuge, and fortress unto His kingdom.
webster_full: DIVINE PROTECTION, the doctrine of God’s providential keeping of His people.
He is the refuge and fortress of those who dwell in Him (Psa 91:1–2).
He preserves the soul and the going out and coming in of His own (Psa 121:7–8).
His name is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are safe (Pro 18:10).
The Lord is faithful to stablish and keep His people from evil (2Th 3:3).
scriptures: Psa 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil.
corruption_summary: The presumptuous “hedge of protection” health-wealth teaching corrupts divine protection, promising exemption from all harm and ignoring the cross, martyrdom, and persecution.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the presumptuous health-and-wealth teaching that turns God’s providential keeping into a guarantee of earthly safety, a magic “hedge of protection” that exempts the faithful from sickness, loss, danger, and death. This forgets that the Lord who is a refuge let His prophets be slain, His apostles be martyred, and His Son be crucified. The promise of Psalm 91 is not that no trouble touches the saint, but that the LORD is his refuge through it; the protection is real, yet it is the keeping of providence unto God’s kingdom, not a charm against all earthly harm. To claim immunity from suffering is to presume upon God and to invite the very testing of which Satan spoke when he quoted this psalm to tempt Christ.

The deeper error is that this teaching ignores the cross and the reality of persecution. Scripture promises that all who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution, that the saints overcome by the blood of the Lamb and loved not their lives unto the death. Martyrdom is not a failure of divine protection but its crown; the martyr’s soul is preserved while his body is given up. The dictionary holds that God truly keeps His people — their souls infallibly, their bodies according to His wise will — and that the deepest protection is His pledge to bring them safely home, even through the fire and the sword.
roots_summary: God providentially keeps His people as shield and refuge, infallibly in soul, wisely in body.
roots_lines: Protegere — Latin, “to cover, to shield.”
Refuge — the LORD a refuge and fortress to His own (Psa 91:2).
Preservation — He preserves the soul from all evil (Psa 121:7).
Strong tower — the righteous run into His name and are safe (Pro 18:10).
Faithfulness — the Lord keeps His people from evil (2Th 3:3).
usage: Trust the LORD as your refuge through trouble; He does not promise exemption from it.
God’s keeping is sure for the soul and wise for the body, unto His kingdom.
Martyrdom is not a failure of protection but its crown; the soul is kept though the body fall.

etymology: From the Old English hærfest, “autumn, reaping”; a scriptural figure for both the gathering of souls into the kingdom and the final judgment at the end of the world.
biblical_def: The harvest is a great scriptural figure with a twofold meaning: the present ingathering of souls through the preaching of the gospel, and the final reaping of the world in judgment at the last day. Christ saw the multitudes and was moved with compassion, saying, “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few; pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Mat 9:37–38). He bade His disciples lift up their eyes, for “the fields… are white already to harvest” (Joh 4:35), the gospel harvest of souls ripe for gathering. Yet the harvest is also the end: in the parable of the tares, He declared, “The harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels” (Mat 13:39), when the wheat shall be gathered into the barn and the tares burned. And in the Revelation a voice cries to the One on the cloud, “Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe” (Rev 14:15). Thus the harvest sets before the church both her labour and her hope: she sows the seed of the word now, praying the Lord of the harvest to gather souls; and she waits for the final reaping, when Christ shall separate the wheat from the tares and gather His own into His everlasting garner. The harvest is the Lord’s; the increase is His to give.
webster_summary: The scriptural figure of both the gospel ingathering of souls and the final judgment at the end of the world.
webster_full: THE HARVEST, a figure of the gospel ingathering and the final judgment.
The harvest is plenteous; the Lord of the harvest sends labourers (Mat 9:37–38).
The fields are white already to harvest (Joh 4:35).
The harvest is the end of the world; the reapers are the angels (Mat 13:39).
The sickle is thrust in when the harvest of the earth is ripe (Rev 14:15).
scriptures: Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
Joh 4:35
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels.

And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to him that sat on the cloud, Thrust in thy sickle, and reap: for the time is come for thee to reap; for the harvest of the earth is ripe.
corruption_summary: Triumphalist church-growth pragmatism corrupts the doctrine of the harvest, counting numbers and methods over true conversion and leaving the increase to man rather than to the Lord of the harvest.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the church-growth pragmatism that measures the harvest by visible numbers and clever methods, treating souls as statistics and the increase of the church as the fruit of marketing rather than the work of God. It counts decisions, baptisms, and attendance as proof of harvest, while the true grain — repentance, faith, the new birth, perseverance — is left unexamined. But Christ teaches that the harvest is the Lord’s; the labourers are sent by Him, and the increase is His to give (1Co 3:6–7). A swelling crowd is not necessarily a harvest of wheat; the field holds tares as well, and only the final reaping will tell them apart.

This pragmatism forgets the second meaning of the harvest, the end of the world, when Christ Himself separates the wheat from the tares (Mat 13:39). The church that counts heads as conversions may gather many tares with the wheat and mistake numerical success for spiritual fruit. The dictionary holds that the harvest is twofold and wholly the Lord’s: His people sow the seed of the word in faithfulness and pray Him to gather souls, but they do not manufacture the increase, nor judge the harvest by the world’s measure of size and speed. True conversion, not numbers, is the wheat; and the final reaping, not the latest method, is the test.
roots_summary: A twofold figure: the gospel ingathering of souls now and the final reaping of the world at the end.
roots_lines: Hærfest — Old English, “autumn, reaping.”
Ingathering — the harvest is plenteous, the labourers few (Mat 9:37).
Ripe fields — lift up your eyes, the fields are white (Joh 4:35).
End of the world — the harvest is the last day (Mat 13:39).
Final reaping — the sickle thrust into the ripe earth (Rev 14:15).
usage: Pray the Lord of the harvest to send labourers; the increase is His to give, not ours to manufacture.
A swelling crowd is not yet a harvest of wheat; the field holds tares until the final reaping.
Sow the word in faithfulness and leave the harvest to God, who alone makes the seed to grow.

etymology: From the Latin tribulatio, “a pressing, an affliction”; the doctrine of the afflictions through which God brings His people into His kingdom.
biblical_def: Tribulation is the doctrine of the afflictions through which God appoints His people to pass on their way to glory. It is no accident of the Christian life but its very road: Paul and Barnabas confirmed the souls of the disciples, “exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22). The Lord warned His own plainly, yet comforted them in the same breath: “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” (Joh 16:33). Far from being a sign of God’s displeasure, tribulation is the furnace in which He works the graces of His people: “tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope” (Rom 5:3–5). And in the great vision of heaven, the redeemed multitude is named as those “which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14). Thus the church is taught to expect affliction, not to be surprised by it as though some strange thing happened, but to count it the appointed path. Through tribulation God conforms His people to Christ, who Himself entered His glory through suffering; and the same tribulation that presses them now is working a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. The kingdom is entered through the cross, never around it.
webster_summary: The doctrine that God brings His people into His kingdom through much affliction, conformed to the suffering Christ.
webster_full: TRIBULATION, the afflictions through which God brings His people to glory.
We must through much tribulation enter the kingdom of God (Act 14:22).
In the world the saints have tribulation, but Christ has overcome it (Joh 16:33).
Tribulation worketh patience, experience, and hope (Rom 5:3–5).
The redeemed come out of great tribulation, robes washed in the blood of the Lamb (Rev 7:14).
scriptures: Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
Rom 5:3
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;
Rev 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
corruption_summary: Dispensational pre-tribulation escapism corrupts the doctrine of tribulation, promising the church a secret exit from affliction by way of a 19th-century novelty.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is dispensational pre-tribulation escapism, which teaches that the church will be secretly raptured away before a coming great tribulation, so that the saints are promised an exit from affliction rather than a passage through it. This rests upon dispensational premillennialism, a system unknown to the church for eighteen centuries, devised in the nineteenth by John Nelson Darby and popularized by the Scofield Reference Bible. No Reformation confession contains it; it is a novelty, not the faith once delivered. The dictionary rejects it as the voice-lock requires, naming it for what it is: a recent invention superimposed upon the plain teaching that “we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Act 14:22).

The error is not merely chronological but pastoral and deadly. It teaches the church to expect escape where Christ taught her to expect affliction: “In the world ye shall have tribulation” (Joh 16:33). It cannot account for the great multitude in heaven who “came out of great tribulation” (Rev 7:14), nor for the apostles who endured it, nor for the suffering church in every age and land. By promising an exit, it leaves believers unprepared to suffer and tempts them to count affliction a sign that something has gone wrong. The dictionary holds the historic faith: the kingdom is entered through the cross, tribulation is the appointed path, and God uses it to work patience, experience, and hope in His people, conforming them to the Christ who Himself entered glory through suffering.
roots_summary: God brings His people into the kingdom through much affliction, conforming them to the suffering Christ.
roots_lines: Tribulatio — Latin, “a pressing, an affliction.”
The road — through much tribulation into the kingdom (Act 14:22).
Comfort — Christ has overcome the world (Joh 16:33).
Fruit — tribulation worketh patience and hope (Rom 5:3–5).
The robed multitude — come out of great tribulation (Rev 7:14).
usage: Expect affliction as the appointed path; be not surprised as though some strange thing happened.
Tribulation is the furnace in which God works patience, experience, and hope in His people.
The kingdom is entered through the cross, never around it; seek no secret exit from suffering.
